$comment: Where each host keeps the tools this project runs on it.

Firmware is built only in the pinned container (docs/build-container.md), so a bench needs bossac, binutils to read images, and optionally a host C compiler for the native test harnesses. The compiler and SAM core entries also describe the image.
This file is COMMITTED and shared: adding a host means adding a search
pattern here, not editing CMake or a script. It follows the same rule as
requirements-dev.txt - the declaration travels, the installed bytes do not.
Each tool lists glob patterns per platform, tried in order; the first match
that exists and contains the named executable wins. Platform keys are
Placeholders: {repo} = repository root, {home} = the user's home directory.
Patterns always name a DIRECTORY; 'requires' is the executable inside it
For a machine this file does not describe, create toolchains.local.json
with the same shape - it is gitignored, searched first, and only needs the
tools that differ. Prefer adding a pattern here if the layout is one another
teammate could plausibly have; keep local overrides for genuinely odd paths.
ARM_TOOLCHAIN_DIR in the environment, or -DARM_TOOLCHAIN_DIR, still wins

arm_toolchain.what: The bin/ holding arm-none-eabi-gcc. Inside the build image this is the compiler, and ARM_TOOLCHAIN_DIR names it ahead of any pattern. On a bench it is the binutils (readelf, nm) that read an image's compiler and layout into the flash log; no bench builds firmware with it
reject_why: arduino:sam bundles gcc 4.8.3 from 2014. Track B is deliberately not
built with it, and it is on PATH-adjacent disk on any machine with the
Arduino IDE installed, so it is refused by pattern rather than by luck.
note: On macOS use the xPack build: ARM's own darwin-x86_64 build links cc1
against Homebrew's zstd at an absolute path and dies in dyld on a machine
without Homebrew, while reporting a version happily from the driver.
That is a macOS packaging defect, not a verdict on ARM's toolchain -
ARM's mingw-w64 build is self-contained and is what Windows uses here.

bossac.what: SAM flash programmer, shipped with the Arduino sam core

arduino_sam_core.what: Track A's vendored source: the installed arduino:sam hardware core. Only its SOURCES are used - no arduino-cli invocation and no bundled 2014 compiler (see cmake/track_a.cmake).
requires_why: A directory, not an executable. Both resolvers join `requires` onto the
hit and test for a file, so a nested path works and is the honest check:
the core's own header is what track_a.cmake actually needs to exist.
version_why: The patterns name 1.6.12 rather than globbing sam/*. linux-x1's point,
and it is right: a bench silently building against a different core is
the mixed-revision hazard the clean-build rule exists for, and cross-
bench figures are comparable only if the vendored source is the same.
A bench on another version adds a pattern here or a toolchains.local
.json - which leaves a trace, where a glob would not.
where_why: Linux only, because the build image is the only place Track A is
compiled: its HOME holds the core at exactly this path. A bench flashes
the image and needs no core sources.

host_cc.what: Host C compiler for the board-free framer seam test (tests/test_framer_close.py), which builds and RUNS its harness. GNU only - see CLAUDE.md, MSVC cannot build lib/due_shared. Only consulted when cc/gcc/clang are not already on PATH, which is the Windows case.
